audit_comment: The DSG OVERVIEW OF THE UNDERDARK, printed pp. 7-11 (pdf 8-12) - the first DSG content round, the R497 pattern applied to the dungeoneering book: the three natural cave types (limestone, sea, lava), the living/dead cave split, the drip formations, the geothermal ladder with the 1,800-degree lava, the unnatural locale taxonomy (dungeons, mines, burrows, realms) and the five hazard families of the underearth. The load-bearing pins: the pdf = printed + 1 offset (proved by the chapter opener on pdf 7 for printed 6); the three-cave taxonomy; the molten lava temperature of approximately 1,800 F that kills non-fire-resistant creatures on contact; the 10-foot dirt-shoring interval; the realms-deeper-than-a-mile rule; and the living/dead cave mechanics (glisten, sturdy, mud pools vs brittle, dust, rubble, standing-but-not-stagnant water). The DM-section boxes of tools/dsg_gap_report.md are re-grained in the same splice from the DM table of contents pulled at pdf 65, and the perspective-maps section (pp. 124-127) the player TOC missed is opened. Provenance: the tesseract reads (d8-d12 full/tsv/png) on the r503-extraction branch; pdf 9 is the cave-formations illustration plate (labels only).

The pdf-page offset is printed + 1, the same as the WSG. bools.comment: limestone caves are by far the most common type, found mostly where the bedrock is a great shelf of limestone.
bools.name: dovLimestoneMostCommon

bools.comment: dolomite and marble terrain can also serve as an environment for the creation of a limestone cave.
bools.name: dovLimestoneCarbonateBedrock

bools.comment: a limestone cave is created by the erosive and corrosive action of water seeping through rock; rainwater, a dilute carbonic acid from absorbed carbon dioxide, quickly eats away limestone.
bools.name: dovLimestoneAcidErosion

bools.comment: a drop in the water table leaves formerly underwater passages dry and full of air; droughts, floods or terrain movement can shift the flow.
bools.name: dovWaterTableDrainsCave

bools.comment: the inlets or outlets of the water that once flowed through a cave, often tortuously narrow or steep, are the most common entrances to limestone caves.
bools.name: dovLimestoneWaterInletEntrances

bools.comment: a cave grown too large may collapse its ceiling into a sinkhole dropping precipitously from the surface to the cave floor, usable as an entrance for characters willing to do a little rope work.
bools.name: dovSinkholeEntrance

bools.comment: stalactites hang from the ceiling and stalagmites grow upward from the floor, created by slow dripping water that evaporates and leaves mineral deposits; the color ranges from muddy brown to red to a rare pure crystalline white.
bools.name: dovDripFormations

bools.comment: the other cave features are draperies (ruffled-curtain stone sheets), flowstone (falling in tiers like flowing sludge) and rare, delicate gypsum flowers.
bools.name: dovOtherFormations

bools.comment: a cave subject to continuing water seepage is a living cave: its features grow, glisten and shine in light, and are very sturdy; the cave is generally clean and almost dust-free before creatures enter.
bools.name: dovLivingCaveSeepage

bools.comment: in a living cave all low areas not regularly swept by flowing water contain pools of sticky mud, which can be quite deep depending on drainage and shape.
bools.name: dovLivingCaveMud

bools.comment: in a dead cave the water no longer flows: the features do not glisten, grow very weak without constant humidity, become brittle and eventually crumble into dust.
bools.name: dovDeadCaveBrittle

bools.comment: a dead cave is much more likely to be choked with rubble than its living counterpart, and a layer of dust often covers everything.
bools.name: dovDeadCaveRubble

bools.comment: water found in a dead cave has generally been standing for centuries but is very rarely stagnant - the cold temperatures and lack of sunlight see to that.
bools.name: dovDeadCaveWaterNotStagnant

bools.comment: completely water-filled limestone caves generally have smooth, rubble-free passages, though very narrow or tightly winding ones may be difficult or impossible to travel.
bools.name: dovWaterFilledSmooth

bools.comment: sea caves are formed along current or former coastlines where the erosive action of pounding surf gradually wears an entrance into the bedrock.
bools.name: dovSeaCaveSurfCarved

bools.comment: sea caves are generally much smaller than limestone caves, since the waves disperse their energy quickly as they work inward.
bools.name: dovSeaCaveSmaller

bools.comment: sea caves are often partially water-filled; a changing water level can leave one completely submerged with a hidden mouth, or stranded in a cliff far above the surf or many miles inland.
bools.name: dovSeaCaveWaterLevels

bools.comment: sea caves have smooth floors, walls and ceilings with none of the spectacular limestone features, but their relatively easy access makes relics of long-past inhabitants more likely.
bools.name: dovSeaCaveSmoothNoFeatures

bools.comment: a river-bend abrasion cavern, eroded where water pounds the outer bank, resembles a sea cave in most respects.
bools.name: dovRiverbendLikeSeaCave

bools.comment: a lava cave is created when the crust of a flowing lava surface hardens while the molten lava beneath continues to flow away, leaving an air-filled space that may reach considerable size.
bools.name: dovLavaCrustOrigin

bools.comment: lava caves are commonly found in areas of volcanic activity and do not contain the features typical of limestone caves.
bools.name: dovLavaCaveVolcanic

bools.comment: unless in a region of heavy rainfall or at a very low elevation, lava caves may well be completely dry.
bools.name: dovLavaCaveDry

bools.comment: a great many lava caves have no exits to the outside world; their existence can only be discovered by chance excavation or by breaking through a thin crust.
bools.name: dovLavaCaveHiddenExits

bools.comment: earthquake and rockslide chambers, tenuously supported by accumulated rubble, resemble caves but are not true caves; they make good overnight shelters and lairs for hostile animals or monsters.
bools.name: dovQuakeChamberNotTrueCave

bools.comment: geological faulting creates cavities when a large shelf of rock moves and the neighboring rock stays stationary; such caverns are often completely enclosed but may be very large.
bools.name: dovFaultCavityEnclosed

bools.comment: geothermal heat can be encountered in deep caves of any kind but is particularly likely in a lava cave, since lava itself is a carrier of geothermal heat.
bools.name: dovGeothermalInDeepCaves

bools.comment: the glowing crimson flow of molten lava carries heat from the deepest reaches and quickly kills any non-fire-resistant creature forced into contact with it.
bools.name: dovLavaKillsOnContact

bools.comment: even where lava has cooled to a solid crust it is still blisteringly hot, and a character venturing onto it risks breaking through into the infernal heat below.
bools.name: dovLavaCrustBreakRisk

bools.comment: steam can scald or even kill a creature caught in its intense blast; sudden vaporization in high-geothermal areas creates high pressures, and blasts can erupt far from the actual heat source.
bools.name: dovSteamScalds

bools.comment: warm or hot water, a more tolerable form of geothermal heat, ranges from lukewarm to boiling depending on the proximity and intensity of the heat source.
bools.name: dovHotWaterRange

bools.comment: warm or hot air rising through subterranean passages is often an explorer's first warning of approaching geothermal heat.
bools.name: dovWarmAirFirstWarning

bools.comment: dungeons are built by intelligent creatures, each to serve a particular purpose; some are constructed entirely from caves, others use caves as entrances or emergency exits only.
bools.name: dovDungeonPurposeBuilt

bools.comment: dungeon passages generally run within a few hundred feet of the surface; the deeper the dungeon, the harder the task of moving the excavated material out of the way.
bools.name: dovDungeonShallowish

bools.comment: dungeons are generally excavated from a soft rock such as sandstone or limestone - not as hard to excavate as granite, yet still a solid and sturdy support.
bools.name: dovDungeonSoftRock

bools.comment: some dungeons begin as buildings whose ruins are later buried by new buildings until the original layer seems well underground; encountered dungeons may be collapsing, newly excavated, or still under construction.
bools.name: dovRuinsBecomeDungeons

bools.comment: the most common dungeon purposes are jails, hiding places for treasures, lairs for bands of underground creatures, and positions of defense.
bools.name: dovDungeonPurposes

bools.comment: in a world where flying creatures are ever-present, dungeons can prove to be stronger fortresses than castles.
bools.name: dovDungeonStrongerThanCastles

bools.comment: fantasy-world mines are almost always tunnels or shafts; mines developed over centuries by diligent excavators such as dwarves or gnomes can become complicated three-dimensional networks stretching for dozens of miles.
bools.name: dovMineTunnelNetworks

bools.comment: active mines are usually well-guarded; inactive mines - closed for a depleted vein, a disaster or a conflict - often become the lairs of subterranean monsters.
bools.name: dovMineActiveGuarded

bools.comment: burrows are long tunnels generally no bigger in diameter than the creature that created them, often with a widened chamber at the deepest end; usually dug from dirt, but certain creatures such as umber hulks can burrow in solid stone.
bools.name: dovBurrowCreatorSized

bools.comment: realms are vast underground reaches of caverns, dungeons and lofty passages deep beneath the earth, regions of mystery to surface dwellers; the drow, deep gnomes, duergar, kuo-toa and derro live in reaches that never see the light of day.
bools.name: dovRealmsDeepMystery

bools.comment: realms contain cavern networks that might rival an entire nation in size and underground bodies of water as big as any outerworld sea, with islands just as surface seas have.
bools.name: dovRealmNationScale

bools.comment: certain vast realms are best described as wilderness where no cultures flourish, while other areas boast cities and fortresses worthy of the most advanced civilizations; horrific beasts rumored never to venture up to dungeon level are said to live there.
bools.name: dovRealmWildernessToCities

bools.comment: cave-ins, a constant problem under tons of earth and rock, are triggered by erosion or by sudden shocks such as earthquakes or explosions; those underneath suffer falling damage and are often pinned or trapped with little air.
bools.name: dovCaveinTriggers

bools.comment: dungeons are protected against cave-ins by shoring passages with timbers or stone arches, caverns lack such engineered protection, and realms are too vast for it - and so rarely subject to cave-ins, though a realm cave-in rivals the worst hurricane or tidal wave.
bools.name: dovCaveinProtectionSplit

bools.comment: underground flood water has little chance to spread out and disperse; corridors may fill with water, making drowning a virtual certainty for any air-breathing creature caught there.
bools.name: dovFloodNoDispersion

bools.comment: fires threaten underground dwellings in a double sense: they consume combustible objects in their path and also use up the precious oxygen, which exists in finite supply.
bools.name: dovFireDoubleThreat

bools.comment: wood is not a common building material underground - the difficulty of transporting it in and its tendency to rot in damp conditions discourage its use - though shoring up a corridor is much easier with wood than with stone.
bools.name: dovWoodUncommonUnderground

bools.comment: poisonous gases, whether natural (like the sulfur dioxide of volcanic areas), magical or manufactured, menace all oxygen-breathers, and their use as a weapon of war is greatly enhanced in the constricted underearth.
bools.name: dovPoisonGasConfined

bools.comment: volcanoes are a major cause of subterranean fires and poison-gas emissions; often occurring with earthquakes, a volcanic burst can fill inhabited corridors with lava or steam and close off escape passages or popular transportation routes.
bools.name: dovVolcanoDamage

consts.name: dovCaveTypeCount

consts.comment: molten lava has a temperature of approximately 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit and quickly kills any non-fire-resistant creature forced into contact with it.
consts.name: dovLavaTempF

consts.comment: a dungeon excavated from dirt requires constant shoring up, at least at 10-foot intervals, to prevent cave-ins.

consts.name: dovRealmShallowMi

prev_record: - R502 LANDED 2026-10-16: commit 4681d11 (census 427, pushed
77d39de..4681d11), the WSG CAMP-CHAIN FOLD - the fourth seam round, the R499
fold pattern applied to the camp chapter: one campsite flows through six
landed headers - the rest quality and Table 38 fire (rules/wsgfire.h R474),
the fire starting and fuel rules (rules/wsgfuel.h R475), the wildfire rules
(rules/wsgblaze.h R476), the tent quality system (rules/wsgsleep.h R473), the
natural shelters (rules/wsgshelter.h R471) and the R499 temperature chain
re-read for the seam. Pinned as rules/wsgcampfold.h (prefix wmc, 63 inlines:
53 consts + 10 bools, no grids, NO gap flips - the report stays 186/0).
FINDINGS: the wildfire hour (the 6-turn uncontrollable bar equals the 6 turns
per hour - a fire left alone for exactly one hour becomes uncontrollable); the
two-header refuel identity (the Table 38 small-fire refuel interval and the
fuel-header grace period are the same 3 turns); the twenty-mph triple
agreement (the small fire wind resistance, the rest wind-penalty threshold and
the poor-shelter full-protection example - three headers, one number); the
no-start paradox (no fire starts in wind over 30 mph - exactly the wind a
medium fire would have withstood); the arithmetic-vs-geometric split (the fuel
+6, refuel +3, wind-res +10 and spark +10 ladders are all arithmetic; the
growth ladder 1, 2, 4 is the chain's only doubling); THE R499 TEMPERATURE SEAM
ON BOTH SIDES (the rest cold threshold is the same 0 that opens the dress
below-0 column; the rest hot threshold of 90 opens one degree past the
protected no-damage top of 89, at heat band 18); the flat plate loss (5 hours
in plate rest like 1, 9 rest like 5 - a flat 4-hour loss either way); the tent
leak halves the wind step it cannot stop (5 per 10). Preflight GREEN (R502 WSG
camp chain fold audit: bad 0), rverify GREEN (63 mutants, 0 missed, double-run
clean). Local gates: 50/50 mechanical cross-checks against the six headers.
User-side spec md5 d08adacc36cd2e802aafa0f8b3991d89 differed from both
authored variants (533a6a35... +nl, ea20b948... no-nl) - cosmetic, the
standing class. Spec published as the new canvas r502-splice. THE FOLD ARC
COMPLETE: R499- R502, four clean lands (temperature, swimmer motion,
movement/fall, camp), 198 mutants all caught. The WSG mechanical seams are
exhausted; the natural next move is the DSG (Dungeoneer's Survival Guide) as
the next book, opening a fresh pin arc with its own gap report.
